# Weekly Multi-Asset Watchlist Briefing

This week’s tape was defined by a sharp divergence beneath relatively orderly index-level price action, with pronounced factor and subsector rotations playing out across semiconductors, software infrastructure, fintech, and materials. Within the watchlist, leadership skewed toward cyclicals and select growth compounders with clear fundamental or thematic support, while crowded quality and perceived “bond proxies” saw episodic de-risking. Hardware-related AI beneficiaries in memory and compute again outperformed, led by double-digit weekly gains in names such as Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Micron Technology (MU), while other parts of the semiconductor complex, including POET Technologies (POET), Credo Technology (CRDO), and Broadcom (AVGO), faced meaningful drawdowns. On the software side, the market rewarded idiosyncratic execution in observability and collaboration, as Datadog (DDOG) and Atlassian (TEAM) rallied strongly, even as parts of cloud infrastructure and fintech traded as funding-sensitive proxies and lagged. The macro backdrop remained dominated by the push-pull between sticky services inflation and a decelerating growth impulse, with rates volatility driving factor performance more than any single data release, and leaving investors focused on micro-level dispersion, positioning, and upcoming policy and data catalysts rather than a clear top-down trend.

## Market Overview

The broad equity backdrop this week can best be characterized as a market in transition from a narrow, megacap-led advance toward a more rotational, dispersion-driven regime. While index-level performance was not extreme relative to the preceding month, the underlying cross-currents across sectors and factor styles were unusually intense, particularly within technology, financials, and cyclically exposed value. Within the technology complex, the advance in select AI hardware and infrastructure names contrasted with weakness in several prior leadership pockets, highlighting that investors are now differentiating more finely between direct beneficiaries of incremental capex, valuation-stretched AI narratives, and names where expectations may already discount multi-year adoption curves.

Semiconductors remained at the center of this narrative. The week saw AMD advance by approximately 12.0 percent on the week and 20.8 percent over the trailing month, underscoring continued enthusiasm for its positioning in high-performance computing and AI accelerators. POET Technologies, by contrast, fell about 16.8 percent over the week and is down modestly over the month, suggesting investors are rotating away from higher-risk, earlier-stage semicap stories toward proven platforms with stronger near-term revenue visibility. Micron added about 10.2 percent for the week and nearly 39.4 percent for the month, reflecting the ongoing repricing of high-bandwidth memory and AI server demand into the stock. These crosscurrents generated significant intra-sector dispersion, even as the broader narrative around AI capex remained constructive.

In software and internet, the market displayed an equally pronounced preference for specific execution stories and improving margin frameworks. Datadog gained roughly 9.3 percent on the week, while Atlassian advanced about 11.1 percent, in both cases building on the notion that usage-based models are stabilizing and that cloud optimization headwinds are gradually abating. At the same time, some structurally strong franchises in adjacent spaces struggled. Oracle declined by about 7.3 percent on the week, indicating investor concerns around the timing and magnitude of cloud database and infrastructure monetization relative to expectations. In consumer-facing digital and e-commerce, Shopify fell approximately 11.5 percent this week and about 18.6 percent over the past month, pointing to a more cautious stance on small and medium business spending, competitive intensity, and the durability of pandemic-era gains.

Financials and fintech names on the watchlist reflected a more defensive risk posture among investors, particularly toward credit-sensitive and regulatory-sensitive models. Coinbase declined by around 10.0 percent on the week and just under 10 percent over the month, reflecting a combination of lower crypto trading volumes and renewed concerns around the regulatory environment. Within traditional and hybrid financials, Capital One fell by about 9.1 percent on the week and 12.5 percent over the month, while Morgan Stanley declined by roughly 5.3 percent this week. This pattern is consistent with a market that is beginning to price in the possibility of slower consumer credit growth, tighter net interest margins at the margin, and a more uneven capital markets backdrop despite pockets of strength in equity issuance and structured products.

Finally, the macro-sensitive materials and energy complex on the watchlist exhibited a constructive tone. The Mosaic Company gained about 9.3 percent on the week and 18.8 percent over the month, while Newmont and Agnico Eagle advanced approximately 8.9 percent and 8.6 percent, respectively, for the week and high-teens percentages over the month. These moves suggest that investors are increasingly willing to hold inflation-hedging and late-cycle assets alongside growth exposures, especially as real yields oscillate and the path of central bank policy normalization remains uncertain. Against this tapestry of rotations, the key takeaway for portfolio construction is that dispersion is high, factor leadership is unstable, and the opportunity set is rich for stock pickers with clear theses around AI infrastructure, software monetization, financial tightening, and commodity cycles.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

Sector and style leadership this week was most visible in the sharp intra-tech rotation and the relative outperformance of certain cyclical and defensive pockets. Within the semiconductor bucket, performance bifurcated sharply between AI-levered memory and compute names versus more idiosyncratic or earlier-stage stories. AMD, with a roughly 12.0 percent weekly gain and more than 20 percent appreciation over the month, exemplified sustained investor conviction in its roadmap for data center GPUs, AI accelerators, and high-performance CPUs. Micron’s approximate 10.2 percent weekly and nearly 39.4 percent monthly gains reflected accelerating expectations around high-bandwidth memory demand for AI servers and a normalization of the DRAM and NAND pricing cycle. By contrast, POET’s roughly 16.8 percent weekly decline and modest monthly loss, along with Credo’s approximately 11.8 percent weekly and similar monthly drawdowns, highlight that not all AI-adjacent or connectivity names are being treated equally; markets are demanding clear visibility into revenue scale, margin trajectory, and customer pipelines.

Other semiconductor and adjacent hardware names also underscored this rotation. SNDK advanced about 14.6 percent on the week and nearly 89.5 percent over the trailing month, a remarkable move that signals intense repositioning around storage-exposed vehicles perceived as structurally tied to data growth. Arm Holdings gained approximately 9.7 percent during the week and about 4.0 percent for the month, reflecting ongoing enthusiasm for its licensing model in a world of proliferating AI and edge compute designs. Meanwhile, Broadcom fell around 9.0 percent this week and about 8.6 percent over the month, suggesting a period of consolidation after a strong multi-quarter run and potentially some investor concern about the integration path and cyclicality embedded in its diversified portfolio. SiTime’s roughly 7.7 percent weekly decline and 9.3 percent monthly loss further reinforce that highly specialized semiconductor companies can face outsized volatility when the market reassesses near-term demand visibility.

Software infrastructure exhibited a more constructive, though nuanced, pattern of leadership. Datadog’s roughly 9.3 percent weekly gain, together with GitLab’s approximate 6.6 percent rise, underscored investor appetite for tools central to observability, DevOps, and modern cloud-native development workflows. Samsara, by contrast, fell about 8.0 percent this week and 12.2 percent over the month, indicating some fatigue around high-multiple applied AI names that priced in very long-duration growth. Nutanix’s approximately 6.4 percent weekly decline and 17.7 percent monthly drop underscore that hybrid cloud and on-prem-to-cloud transition stories remain sensitive to enterprise spending trends, deal cycles, and ongoing debates about the optimal architecture for AI-era workloads. Cloudflare and Ciena, each declining by around 5.8 percent and 5.9 percent respectively, add to the sense that markets are more cautious on names heavily levered to network capex cycles and usage growth where valuation already embeds substantial future penetration.

Within application software, the market rewarded targeted execution and operating leverage in some names, even as it de-rated others with less near-term operating visibility. Atlassian’s weekly performance of about 11.1 percent, despite being down approximately 18.2 percent over the month, suggests that investors see the recent drawdown as at least partly overdone given the company’s embedded position in developer and knowledge worker workflows. Twilio’s roughly 7.8 percent weekly gain, despite a near 8.6 percent decline over the month, similarly points to selective risk-taking in turnaround and self-help stories where valuation has compressed and management is emphasizing profitability. Freshworks, up about 6.8 percent this week, benefited from continued execution in lower-cost customer experience and IT service management software. At the same time, Oracle’s approximately 7.3 percent weekly loss, Zoom’s roughly 6.0 percent gain paired with a modest monthly decline, and Hims & Hers’ approximately 5.6 percent weekly pullback highlight the market’s shifting evaluation of subscription durability, growth-versus-margin trade-offs, and competitive dynamics across verticals.

Fintech and broader financials on the watchlist experienced a synchronized drawdown that is consistent with tightening financial conditions and growing investor focus on credit quality and regulatory risk. Coinbase’s roughly 10.0 percent weekly and 9.5 percent monthly decline captured both the beta to digital asset prices and idiosyncratic legal and policy overhangs. Capital One’s approximately 9.1 percent weekly and 12.5 percent monthly declines, along with similar magnitude moves in names like Synchrony Financial and Affirm over the month, suggest heightened concerns about consumer delinquencies, revolving credit growth, and the trajectory of underwriting standards. Morgan Stanley and large universal banks such as JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs, all posting mid-single-digit weekly declines, underline that the market is not yet ready to pay up for rate-sensitive balance sheets while the path of policy rates and the slope of the yield curve remain in flux.

In contrast, materials and select energy and industrials exposures generated strong positive returns, reflecting both idiosyncratic factors and macro hedging demand. In the materials bucket, Mosaic’s approximately 9.3 percent weekly and 18.8 percent monthly gains, alongside Newmont’s roughly 8.9 percent weekly and 18.7 percent monthly advances and Agnico Eagle’s similar high-single-digit weekly and near high-teens monthly appreciation, indicate that investors are allocating capital toward inflation-sensitive, late-cycle assets. Generac, which rallied about 7.6 percent on the week and almost 22.9 percent over the month, benefitted from ongoing interest in grid resilience and distributed generation themes. Devon Energy’s approximately 6.7 percent weekly gain and similar monthly performance underline that E&P names with disciplined capital return frameworks can attract flows as late-cycle beneficiaries even in a more volatile commodity price environment. Meanwhile, Sable Offshore’s roughly 10.2 percent weekly decline, despite modest monthly gains, demonstrates that higher-risk offshore or project-heavy names remain exposed to swings in sentiment around capital intensity and project timing.

Consumer and digital commerce names on the watchlist reflected an increasingly nuanced market view around discretionary demand and competitive landscape. Shopify’s roughly 11.5 percent weekly and 18.6 percent monthly decline, juxtaposed with Wix’s approximately 10.4 percent weekly gain despite a mid-teens monthly loss, suggests that investors are differentiating between platforms on the basis of their merchant mix, pricing power, and exposure to smaller, more vulnerable cohorts. McCormick’s approximately 9.3 percent weekly and 11.8 percent monthly decline highlights that even perceived defensive staples can underperform when valuation is stretched and volume growth softens. PVH’s roughly 5.1 percent weekly and 11.0 percent monthly losses indicate the market’s skepticism toward more cyclical apparel names amid uneven consumer demand. By contrast, Unilever’s approximate 3.9 percent weekly gain and Clorox’s roughly 3.2 percent weekly rise show that certain larger-cap staples with clearer cost control and brand power can still serve as havens within a choppy macro environment.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

Focusing on the most significant watchlist movers provides a useful lens into how the market is differentiating between narratives, balance sheets, and exposure to key secular themes. The standout positive movers this week include SNDK, AMD, Micron, Datadog, Atlassian, Wix, Mosaic, Newmont, Agnico Eagle, Fortinet, Braze, Generac, and several others that enjoyed high-single to low-double-digit gains. SNDK’s approximately 14.6 percent weekly rise and nearly 89.5 percent monthly gain are especially notable, signifying a dramatic upward repricing of the company’s earnings power and strategic positioning within data storage. The scale of the monthly move implies that investors have embraced a thesis centered on accelerating data proliferation, AI-related storage requirements, and improved pricing dynamics, while also reflecting positioning dynamics as short interest is forced to cover into strength.

AMD’s roughly 12.0 percent weekly and 20.8 percent monthly advances continue a multi-quarter trend of investors rewarding those chip designers most directly exposed to AI compute demand. The stock’s strength this week likely reflects increasing confidence in the company’s GPU and accelerator offerings, the breadth of hyperscaler and enterprise engagements, and the potential for AI-related revenue to offset any cyclical softness in client or gaming. Micron’s performance, with about 10.2 percent weekly and 31.6 percent to nearly 39.4 percent monthly gains across the memory and storage peer group, underscores how deeply the market has shifted in its view of memory fundamentals. Investors are now willing to underwrite a scenario in which high-bandwidth memory demand for AI servers structurally tightens supply-demand balances and supports a higher mid-cycle profitability level than previously assumed.

On the software side, Datadog’s approximately 9.3 percent weekly rise, against a modest mid-single-digit monthly decline, suggests the market is reassessing its prior caution around usage-based models. The company’s role as a unified observability and monitoring platform across cloud environments positions it as a key beneficiary of both AI-driven workloads and ongoing digital transformation. Atlassian’s about 11.1 percent weekly gain, despite a near 18.2 percent monthly drawdown, can be interpreted as evidence that the recent de-rating may have gone too far in light of the company’s durable positioning across collaboration, developer, and IT workflows. Investors appear to be re-engaging as management continues to articulate a clearer path toward margin expansion and more predictable monetization.

In digital commerce and marketing technology, Wix and Braze each delivered strong weekly performance. Wix’s approximately 10.4 percent weekly advance, even with a roughly 16.1 percent monthly decline, reflects investors’ renewed appreciation of its monetization levers, from subscriptions to payments and value-added services, especially as it executes across both small business and professional cohorts. Braze’s roughly 9.1 percent weekly rise, contrasted with an almost 29.9 percent monthly loss, underscores how quickly sentiment can swing for high-growth SaaS names. After a sharp de-rating that priced in macro headwinds and customer budget scrutiny, any sign of resiliency in customer engagement software demand or improved unit economics can catalyze sharp relief rallies.

Among the more defensive or cyclical beneficiaries, the materials complex stood out. Mosaic’s roughly 9.3 percent weekly and 18.8 percent monthly gains, alongside Newmont’s approximately 8.9 percent weekly and 18.7 percent monthly and Agnico Eagle’s roughly 8.6 percent weekly and 18.3 percent monthly performance, illustrate a market increasingly willing to hold exposure to commodities and precious metals as both inflation hedges and late-cycle plays. The strong performance in these names likely reflects a combination of firm commodity prices, improved cost discipline, and perhaps a modestly weaker growth outlook that favors assets tied to store-of-value narratives. Generac’s about 7.6 percent weekly and 22.9 percent monthly rise results from its leverage to climate-related volatility, grid resilience spending, and the secular adoption of backup power and energy management systems.

On the negative side, POET, Shopify, Credo, Abbott, Sable Offshore, Coinbase, Capital One, Morgan Stanley, and several others were notable underperformers. POET’s approximately 16.8 percent weekly decline and modest monthly loss indicate that the market is increasingly discriminating between early-stage semiconductor and photonics stories, rewarding those with clear revenue ramps while punishing those with longer-dated commercialization. Shopify’s roughly 11.5 percent weekly and 18.6 percent monthly decline signals concerns over the sensitivity of its small and medium business merchant base to macro headwinds, as well as elevated competitive intensity in core e-commerce and payments. Credo’s about 11.8 percent weekly and 11.3 percent monthly decline emphasizes that connectivity and networking names with exposure to hyperscaler capex may be subject to higher volatility as investors constantly re-calibrate the timing and magnitude of AI infrastructure spending.

Abbott’s approximately 11.8 percent weekly and 13.9 percent monthly decline stands out within health care. This drawdown suggests that even high-quality medtech and diagnostics franchises are not immune to valuation compression when growth expectations are recalibrated, or when investors rotate toward other parts of health care perceived as having cleaner near-term catalysts. Sable Offshore’s roughly 10.2 percent weekly decline, despite a modest 5.8 percent monthly gain, shows the vulnerability of project-intensive energy names to swings in sentiment around regulatory and capital deployment risks. Coinbase’s about 10.0 percent weekly and 9.5 percent monthly losses, together with Capital One’s approximately 9.1 percent weekly and 12.5 percent monthly declines, reflect stress points within the broader financial complex as markets grapple with the implications of tighter monetary policy, evolving regulatory frameworks, and potential credit normalization.

This week did not feature major upcoming earnings within the next two weeks for the watchlist constituents, which is unusual relative to more typical weeks heavy with micro-level catalysts. The absence of near-term earnings reports places greater emphasis on macro data, policy guidance, and intra-quarter indicators such as channel checks, pricing commentary, and management conferences. In such an environment, price moves are more a function of positioning, factor flows, and revisions to intermediate-term expectations than immediate earnings surprises. For portfolio managers, this underscores the importance of scenario analysis around macro variables, as well as a close reading of alternative data and qualitative indicators, rather than anchoring near-term positioning solely on forthcoming quarterly reports.

## Macro & Rates Environment

Although explicit high-frequency macro numbers are not provided here, market price action across sectors and factor styles offers clues about how investors are interpreting the growth and inflation backdrop. The outperformance of materials and precious metals names, including Mosaic, Newmont, and Agnico Eagle, suggests that investors remain attentive to inflation risks and see value in assets that can potentially hedge unexpected price pressures. The strong performance of these names over both the week and month indicates that this is not merely a short-lived tactical trade, but rather a more sustained allocation pattern consistent with a late-cycle environment in which inflation is sticky and central banks must balance the risk of overtightening against the risk of doing too little.

At the same time, the weakness in several financials and fintech names can be interpreted through the lens of concerns about the interest rate environment and credit cycle. The drawdowns in Capital One, Synchrony, and Affirm point toward apprehension about consumer credit quality, particularly in unsecured lending and subprime segments, as higher borrowing costs strain household balance sheets. The declines in Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and Goldman Sachs suggest that investors are cautious on bank net interest margins and fee income, especially if yield curves remain compressed and capital markets activity fails to fully offset pressure on lending businesses. This pattern is consistent with a macro regime where policy rates are restrictive enough to slow credit growth, but where the timing and magnitude of future easing remain uncertain.

The performance of rate-sensitive growth and defensives offers further insight. Some long-duration growth names, particularly those tied to AI infrastructure build-out and mission-critical software, continued to perform well despite the macro uncertainty. AMD, Micron, Datadog, and Atlassian all posted strong weekly gains, implying that investors remain willing to look through near-term macro noise when secular growth narratives are deemed robust and underpinned by tangible demand. Conversely, certain defensive consumer staples, such as McCormick, saw meaningful drawdowns despite their perceived resilience. McCormick’s roughly 9.3 percent weekly and 11.8 percent monthly decline suggests that valuations in some defensive names may have become too rich relative to their growth prospects, prompting investors to rotate into other late-cycle plays with more operating leverage or inflation hedging characteristics.

Within fixed income and rates-sensitive sectors, health care provides an instructive case study. UnitedHealth’s approximately 7.6 percent weekly and 8.8 percent monthly gain points to renewed confidence in managed care fundamentals and the ability of diversified health care insurers to navigate reimbursement and policy risk. Abbott’s double-digit weekly and high-teens monthly decline, however, shows that medtech and diagnostics names remain exposed to concerns around procedure volumes, pricing pressure, and reimbursement dynamics, particularly if real incomes are squeezed and public and private payers intensify cost control efforts. The divergence between these health care subsectors suggests that markets are differentiating more finely between business models based on their sensitivity to policy, utilization, and capital markets.

The rotation into materials and select industrials also hints at market expectations for the real economy. Generac’s roughly 7.6 percent weekly and 22.9 percent monthly advance, Devon’s about 6.7 percent weekly gain, and CF Industries’ approximately 6.5 percent weekly and 19.1 percent monthly rise suggest that investors see continued capital spending on infrastructure, energy, and climate resilience as a durable theme, even if aggregate growth moderates. These exposures can benefit from both higher nominal growth and targeted policy support. At the same time, the decline in Sable Offshore and the mixed performance in airlines such as United Airlines, which fell about 5.1 percent on the week and 6.2 percent over the month, highlight that more operationally leveraged or regulation-heavy cyclicals remain vulnerable to any deterioration in the growth outlook or cost pressures.

For portfolio construction, the macro takeaway is that the market is still in the process of discovering a new equilibrium between growth, inflation, and policy. The price action suggests that investors are neither fully embracing a soft-landing, disinflationary Goldilocks scenario nor positioning for an imminent hard landing. Instead, positioning appears bar-belled: investors maintain exposure to structural growth and AI beneficiaries, while simultaneously adding to late-cycle value, commodities, and health care services, and trimming exposure to rate-sensitive financials and certain defensives where valuations are no longer compelling. In this environment, the opportunity lies in owning companies with self-help levers, pricing power, and balance sheet resilience, while underweighting those whose earnings power is overly reliant on benign macro assumptions.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)

AMD remains one of the most closely watched names on the watchlist, and its performance this week reinforces its status as a central beneficiary of the AI compute cycle. The stock’s approximately 12.0 percent weekly gain and 20.8 percent appreciation over the month underscore how quickly sentiment has shifted back in its favor after periods of consolidation. Investors are increasingly focused on AMD’s growing portfolio of GPUs and accelerators targeting data center AI workloads, as well as its competitive positioning against incumbent leaders in high-performance computing. The narrative is supported by a view that hyperscalers and large enterprises will require multiple vendors to secure supply, optimize cost, and avoid over-reliance on any single architecture.

From a fundamental perspective, the key debates around AMD revolve around the trajectory of AI-related revenue ramp, the sustainability of gross margin expansion, and the degree to which AI can offset cyclicality in more mature segments such as client CPUs and gaming. The recent share price strength suggests that the market is assigning increasing probability to scenarios in which AI-related revenue becomes a substantial portion of data center sales over the next several years, while also assuming that AMD can sustain strong execution on product roadmaps and software ecosystems. Risks include potential supply constraints, competitive responses from incumbents and emerging players, and any delay in customer deployments. For portfolio managers, the stock represents a high-beta expression of the AI compute thesis and warrants sizing discipline, but its role as a core growth allocation within semiconductors remains intact.

### Micron Technology (MU)

Micron’s performance this week, with an approximate 10.2 percent weekly gain and a robust 39.4 percent monthly advance, illustrates how rapidly sentiment can turn in cyclical industries when the supply-demand balance inflects. The market is increasingly focused on high-bandwidth memory and other memory solutions that are critical to AI servers and data-intensive workloads. Investors see a path whereby AI-related demand tightens supply, supports higher pricing, and raises the mid-cycle earnings power for memory vendors relative to historical norms. The strength of the stock over the past month reflects this repricing, as investors move from a more cautious view anchored in prior downcycles to a more structurally positive outlook.

Key questions for Micron center on the durability of this AI-driven demand boost, the discipline of industry supply responses, and the company’s ability to capitalize on the mix shift toward higher-value products. The stock’s rapid appreciation implies that a meaningful portion of the favorable scenario is already in the price, increasing the sensitivity to any disappointments in pricing, utilization, or capex plans. Nonetheless, within the watchlist, Micron remains a critical barometer for the broader memory and storage cycle and a high-conviction way to express the view that AI will materially reshape the economics of data infrastructure. For investors with a constructive view on AI capex and industry discipline, the name merits continued attention, though position sizing should reflect its cyclical risk profile.

### POET Technologies (POET)

POET’s roughly 16.8 percent weekly decline and modest 1.6 percent monthly loss stand in stark contrast to the broader strength in many AI-levered semiconductor names. This divergence highlights the market’s increasingly discriminating approach toward smaller, earlier-stage companies in the photonics and advanced packaging arenas. While POET is positioned around important themes such as optical interconnects and power-efficient communication within data centers, the absence of a near-term, scaled revenue base makes the stock more vulnerable to shifts in risk appetite and to investor scrutiny over cash runway and commercialization milestones.

For fundamental investors, POET represents a classic high-risk, high-reward exposure. If the company can execute against its product roadmap, demonstrate strong customer traction, and prove its technology in volume deployments, the upside could be significant given its small base. However, the recent price action underscores that markets are unwilling to pay for long-dated optionality in an environment where capital is no longer free and where many other AI beneficiaries offer nearer-term visibility. The name is therefore best suited for portfolios that can absorb higher volatility and that allocate only a modest fraction of risk budget to earlier-stage innovation stories, complementing more established AI infrastructure holdings.

### SNDK and Western Digital (WDC)

SNDK’s approximately 14.6 percent weekly gain and nearly 89.5 percent monthly move, together with Western Digital’s roughly 6.7 percent weekly and 31.6 percent monthly performance, reinforce the notion that storage-exposed equities have entered a powerful rerating phase. The market appears to be extrapolating accelerating demand for both conventional and AI-related storage, as data growth continues unabated and advanced workloads require increasingly sophisticated storage architectures. Investors are also beginning to appreciate the potential for improved pricing, rationalized industry capacity, and portfolio optimization, including strategic alternatives and restructuring.

Within the watchlist, these names provide a complementary way to express a bullish view on AI infrastructure and broader data proliferation, distinct from but related to GPU and memory plays. For SNDK, the magnitude of the recent rally introduces questions about sustainability and the extent to which expectations may be running ahead of fundamentals. For Western Digital, the performance reflects both cyclical recovery and structural narratives around value unlocking. Portfolio managers should recognize that while the risk-reward profile has improved markedly from prior lows, the sector retains its cyclical character and will be sensitive to any slowdown in capex or changes in pricing discipline.

### Datadog (DDOG)

Datadog’s roughly 9.3 percent weekly gain, despite a modest monthly decline, underscores the market’s re-engagement with high-quality infrastructure software franchises that sit at the heart of cloud observability. As enterprises scale AI and modern microservices architectures, the complexity of distributed systems increases, making unified monitoring and logging platforms indispensable. Datadog’s breadth across metrics, logs, tracing, and security, combined with its rapid pace of product innovation, positions it as a central beneficiary of this trend.

The stock’s previous de-rating reflected concerns around consumption moderation as customers optimized cloud spend and tightened budgets. The recent rebound suggests investors are gaining confidence that these headwinds are easing and that normalized growth combined with strong unit economics justifies a premium multiple. Key watchpoints remain the trajectory of net expansion rates, the pace of new logo additions, and the contribution of new modules to overall growth. Within the watchlist, Datadog serves as a core holding for those seeking exposure to cloud, DevOps, and AI-adjacent software infrastructure, with risk skewed toward macro-driven IT spend fluctuations rather than company-specific execution missteps.

### Atlassian (TEAM)

Atlassian posted a roughly 11.1 percent gain this week, though the stock remains down about 18.2 percent over the past month. This rebound after a sharp drawdown captures the tension between concerns over decelerating growth and appreciation of the company’s entrenched position in collaboration and developer tooling. Investors have been reassessing the company’s transition to cloud, its pricing strategy, and the path to margin expansion. The strong weekly performance suggests that some investors view the recent pullback as an opportunity to add exposure to a high-quality franchise at more reasonable valuation levels.

From a thesis perspective, Atlassian’s long-term value proposition is anchored in its ability to serve as a system of record for teams, projects, and development workflows across organizations of varying sizes. While macro headwinds and optimization efforts can weigh on near-term seat expansion and paid conversions, the secular trends toward agile development, DevOps, and digital collaboration remain intact. The key for investors is balancing this structural optimism against realistic assumptions about growth normalization and the timing of margin uplift. Within diversified software allocations, Atlassian can play the role of a durable compounder, albeit with sensitivity to broader growth sentiment and valuation cycles.

### Cloudflare (NET), Ciena (CIEN), and Arista Networks (ANET)

The networking and cloud edge cohort delivered a mixed signal this week. Cloudflare and Ciena each declined by around 5.8 percent and 5.9 percent, respectively, while Arista Networks gained about 5.0 percent. This divergence highlights the market’s nuanced view of where value accrues in the emerging AI and high-performance networking stack. Arista, with its approximately 5.0 percent weekly gain and modest positive monthly performance, continues to benefit from its central role in data center switching and AI cluster networking. Investors see it as a prime beneficiary of sustained hyperscaler capex on networking infrastructure designed to support large AI workloads.

Cloudflare, by contrast, remains a high-multiple name tied to usage growth and expansion into security and developer services. The roughly 5.8 percent weekly decline and about 14.4 percent monthly drop suggest that investors are more skeptical about paying premium valuations in the face of macro uncertainty and intensifying competition in security and edge services. Ciena’s 5.9 percent weekly decline and 4.6 percent monthly loss underscore that optical and telecom capex cycles remain uneven and more susceptible to macro headwinds and carrier spending pauses. For portfolio managers, this group offers a range of risk-reward profiles: Arista as a relatively higher-visibility AI networking beneficiary, Cloudflare as a long-duration growth story with elevated valuation risk, and Ciena as a more cyclical, valuation-sensitive optical and transport equipment provider.

### Shopify (SHOP) and Wix (WIX)

Shopify and Wix, both central to the digital commerce and online presence ecosystem, followed sharply divergent paths this week. Shopify’s roughly 11.5 percent weekly and 18.6 percent monthly declines indicate that investor enthusiasm has cooled meaningfully, driven by concerns over macro-sensitive small and medium business customers, elevated competition, and questions around the sustainability of growth in GMV and ancillary services. The stock’s pullback suggests that prior valuations may have embedded aggressive assumptions about long-term growth and profitability that are now being reassessed in a more cautious macro context.

Wix, on the other hand, advanced approximately 10.4 percent this week, even as it remains down about 16.1 percent over the month. This rebound reflects the market’s recognition of Wix’s improving monetization dynamics, including growth in subscription ARPU and the scaling of payments and value-added services. The stock offers exposure to both the long-tail of small businesses and the professional developer and agency community, providing a more diversified demand base. For portfolio managers, the divergence between Shopify and Wix highlights the need to differentiate between digital commerce platforms based on customer mix, competitive positioning, and the robustness of monetization levers. It also suggests that even within a challenged macro environment, names with clearer self-help stories and more balanced revenue streams can outperform.

### Coinbase (COIN) and Fintech Complex

Coinbase’s approximately 10.0 percent weekly and 9.5 percent monthly decline places it among the more notable underperformers on the watchlist. The stock’s sensitivity to crypto asset prices, trading volumes, and regulatory developments makes it a high-beta proxy for sentiment in digital assets more broadly. The recent move suggests renewed concern about trading activity, potential fee compression, and the regulatory trajectory. In addition, the broader fintech cohort, including Capital One, Morgan Stanley, and other consumer and institutional financial names, also traded lower, with declines ranging from mid- to high-single digits on the week and larger drawdowns over the month in some cases.

These moves are consistent with a market that is re-evaluating the risk-reward across lending, payments, and capital markets businesses in an environment of elevated policy uncertainty and evolving regulatory frameworks. For Coinbase specifically, the investment debate centers on the durability of its core trading franchise, the potential for revenue diversification into staking, custody, and infrastructure services, and the impact of any changes in regulatory classification of digital assets. For the broader fintech and financial cohort, investors must weigh credit cycle risks, funding costs, and structural growth drivers such as digitalization and embedded finance. In aggregate, the sector’s recent underperformance supports a more selective approach, with preference for names that combine strong balance sheets and diversified revenue streams with clear moats in their respective segments.

### Mosaic (MOS), Newmont (NEM), and Agnico Eagle (AEM)

Mosaic, Newmont, and Agnico Eagle together illustrate the appeal of materials and precious metals in the current macro environment. Mosaic’s approximately 9.3 percent weekly and 18.8 percent monthly gains reflect the market’s expectation of robust demand for fertilizers and agricultural inputs, supported by structural food security concerns and potential supply constraints. Newmont’s roughly 8.9 percent weekly and 18.7 percent monthly advance, along with Agnico Eagle’s about 8.6 percent weekly and 18.3 percent monthly performance, suggest that investors are increasingly allocating capital to gold producers as a hedge against macro uncertainty and potential currency debasement.

For diversified portfolios, these names offer both diversification and late-cycle characteristics. Mosaic provides leverage to agricultural markets and can benefit from both higher commodity prices and operational efficiencies. Newmont and Agnico Eagle, as large-scale gold producers, offer geared exposure to gold prices with operational leverage. Their strong recent performance underscores the attractiveness of precious metals as part of a balanced allocation that includes both growth and defensive assets. The key risks revolve around commodity price volatility, operational execution, and geopolitical factors affecting mining operations, but the risk-reward appears more favorable now than during periods of investor apathy toward the space.

### Generac (GNRC)

Generac’s approximately 7.6 percent weekly and 22.9 percent monthly performance positions it as one of the stronger industrial names on the watchlist. The company sits at the nexus of several powerful themes: grid resilience, climate-related volatility, electrification, and distributed energy resources. As extreme weather events and aging grid infrastructure increase the frequency and severity of outages, demand for backup power solutions remains robust. Moreover, Generac’s evolving focus on home energy management, storage, and smart devices adds a layer of secular growth beyond traditional generator sales.

Investors appear to be re-rating the stock as the company demonstrates improved execution, works through prior channel and inventory issues, and articulates a clearer roadmap for integrating hardware and software. The strong recent price action suggests that the market is once again willing to pay for the company’s growth optionality, particularly as it aligns with policy and societal trends supporting resilience and decarbonization. For portfolios, Generac can serve as both a cyclical and secular growth exposure, with idiosyncratic drivers that are somewhat decoupled from broad macro trends, though still sensitive to construction, housing, and capital spending cycles.

### Fortinet (FTNT) and Cybersecurity Cohort

Fortinet’s roughly 8.3 percent weekly gain, with a modest positive monthly performance, indicates that cybersecurity remains a favored theme even amid broader tech rotations. The company’s broad platform and strength in firewalls, secure networking, and integrated security solutions position it well as enterprises upgrade architectures to protect increasingly complex and distributed environments. The market’s willingness to reward Fortinet this week contrasts with more muted or negative moves in other security names on the watchlist, such as Qualys, which fell about 4.3 percent, and Palo Alto Networks, which declined roughly 4.0 percent.

This divergence underscores that investors are refining their preferences within cybersecurity, focusing on those names with a combination of scale, platform breadth, and demonstrated execution. Fortinet’s recent strength suggests confidence in its ability to balance growth with profitability and to capture share in secure networking and SD-WAN. For portfolio managers, the cybersecurity bucket remains an important source of secular growth exposure, but stock selection is critical, as valuation dispersion is significant and the competitive landscape is dynamic.

### UnitedHealth (UNH) and Abbott (ABT)

UnitedHealth and Abbott, both important health care holdings on the watchlist, moved in opposite directions this week, reflecting distinct narratives within the sector. UnitedHealth’s approximately 7.6 percent weekly and 8.8 percent monthly gain signals renewed investor confidence in the managed care model and the company’s ability to navigate reimbursement and policy risk. As a diversified health care insurer with exposure to both commercial and government programs, UnitedHealth benefits from scale, data, and integrated care capabilities that support consistent earnings growth.

Abbott, however, declined roughly 11.8 percent this week and 13.9 percent over the month, making it one of the more notable underperformers. The drawdown likely reflects concerns about the trajectory of procedure volumes, the normalization of demand for certain diagnostics categories, and pricing pressure in a cost-conscious health care environment. The divergence between the two shows that even within defensive sectors like health care, investors are distinguishing sharply between business models, growth trajectories, and risk profiles. For portfolios, UnitedHealth offers defensive growth with policy risk, while Abbott’s recent weakness may present an opportunity for those with a longer time horizon who believe in its innovation pipeline and global footprint, but near-term volatility should be expected.

### Capital One (COF) and Consumer Credit Exposures

Capital One’s approximately 9.1 percent weekly and 12.5 percent monthly decline reflects mounting concerns around the consumer credit cycle. As a major issuer of credit cards and provider of consumer lending, Capital One is highly sensitive to changes in delinquencies, charge-offs, and consumer spending behavior. The stock’s recent drawdown suggests that investors are increasingly wary of potential credit normalization after an extended period of unusually benign loss rates, particularly as higher rates and inflation weigh on household finances.

Within the watchlist, Capital One serves as a bellwether for unsecured consumer credit risk. Its performance, along with weaker trading in Synchrony, Affirm, and related names, indicates that markets are re-pricing the sector to reflect higher loss assumptions and a less favorable risk-adjusted return profile for incremental lending. For risk managers, this argues for a cautious stance on consumer credit exposures, favoring institutions with strong underwriting standards, diversified revenue streams, and ample capital cushions. While the sector will eventually offer attractive entry points as the cycle matures, the current phase remains one of rising, not peaking, credit risk pricing.

## Upcoming Catalysts

With no watchlist earnings scheduled over the next two weeks, the near-term catalyst calendar is dominated by macro data releases, policy communications, industry conferences, and company-specific events such as product launches and capital markets days. In the absence of imminent earnings reports, price action is likely to be driven by incremental information about the macro trajectory, including labor market trends, inflation dynamics, and survey-based indicators of business and consumer sentiment. These data points will inform expectations for central bank policy, which in turn influence discount rates, sector rotation, and factor performance.

For the AI and semiconductor complex, investor attention will remain focused on any announcements or commentary from hyperscalers, large enterprises, and key suppliers regarding AI infrastructure spending plans. Even without formal earnings, industry events, press releases, and informal channel checks can shift expectations for capex intensity and the distribution of spend across GPUs, memory, storage, networking, and power. AMD, Micron, Nvidia, Broadcom, and related names will be highly sensitive to any signals that suggest either acceleration or moderation in AI-related investment. In addition, any news about export controls, supply chain disruptions, or regulatory developments affecting technology hardware could serve as catalysts.

In software and cloud, upcoming catalysts include industry conferences where management teams may provide intra-quarter updates on demand trends, cloud optimization, and the adoption of AI-driven offerings. Names such as Datadog, Atlassian, Cloudflare, GitLab, and Nutanix will be closely watched for commentary on pipeline trends, deal cycles, and customer spending priorities. Investors will also look for signals on how quickly AI features can be monetized and whether they drive incremental demand or primarily support retention and pricing.

For financials and fintech, the key catalysts center on credit and regulatory developments. Any new data points on delinquencies, charge-offs, and reserve builds from peers, as well as commentary from regulators and policymakers on capital standards and consumer protection, could significantly affect sentiment. Coinbase will remain particularly sensitive to any regulatory or legal updates affecting crypto markets, as well as movements in underlying digital asset prices and volumes. Capital One, Synchrony, Affirm, and other consumer credit names will move on any early indicators of stress in specific segments of the borrower base.

In materials, energy, and industrials, catalysts include commodity price moves, policy developments related to energy and infrastructure, and company-specific updates on projects and capital allocation. Mosaic, Newmont, Agnico Eagle, Generac, Devon, and Sable Offshore will all be influenced by macro-level developments, but also by any news related to project timelines, regulatory approvals, and strategic initiatives. Given the strong recent performance of many materials names, any negative surprise on costs, operational execution, or commodity prices could trigger profit-taking.

Finally, in consumer and health care, upcoming catalysts will involve consumer spending data, inflation trends in staples and discretionary categories, and policy developments affecting health care reimbursement and regulation. Shopify, Wix, PVH, McCormick, Unilever, Clorox, UnitedHealth, and Abbott will all be sensitive to signals about demand resilience, input cost pressures, and policy risk. In the absence of earnings, the market will pay close attention to management commentary at conferences and in public appearances to gauge how companies are navigating the current environment.

## What To Watch Next Week

Looking ahead to next week, the primary focus for portfolio managers should be on how the current rotation evolves in response to incremental macro and micro signals. The key question is whether the market continues to favor a bar-belled positioning that pairs structural AI growth and select software with late-cycle materials, industrials, and health care, or whether a new narrative emerges that shifts leadership once again. The pronounced dispersion observed this week suggests that factor and sector positioning are far from settled, creating both risk and opportunity for active managers.

Within semiconductors, it will be important to monitor whether the strong momentum in AMD, Micron, and SNDK can continue, or whether profit-taking emerges after substantial monthly gains. The relative performance of these names versus underperformers like POET, Credo, Broadcom, and SiTime will offer clues about investor conviction in various parts of the AI hardware stack. Any sign of moderation in AI capex enthusiasm could prompt a rotation from the highest-beta beneficiaries into more defensive or value-oriented tech exposures.

In software and cloud, next week will test whether the rebound in Datadog, Atlassian, Twilio, Freshworks, and Zoom has legs, or whether these moves are faded in favor of more defensive growth or value names. Investors will be watching for incremental commentary on demand trends, particularly in Europe and among smaller enterprise and mid-market customers, where macro headwinds can be more acute. The performance of cloud infrastructure names like Cloudflare, Ciena, Arista, and Nutanix will also be informative about how the market is calibrating capex and usage expectations.

For financials and fintech, the key watchpoint is whether this week’s underperformance stabilizes or accelerates. A stabilization in names like Coinbase, Capital One, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, and Goldman Sachs would suggest that much of the recent pessimism has been priced in, while continued weakness could signal rising concerns about credit, regulation, or market liquidity. Within consumer credit, any early indicators of stress in specific cohorts or products could have outsized impact on sentiment.

In materials, energy, and industrials, next week will test the durability of the recent rally. If Mosaic, Newmont, Agnico Eagle, Generac, Devon, CF Industries, and related names can consolidate or extend gains, it would reinforce the thesis that investors are building more structural exposure to late-cycle and inflation-hedging assets. Conversely, a sharp pullback would suggest that recent flows were more tactical in nature. For Generac and other climate and resilience plays, any news related to extreme weather, regulatory support, or infrastructure initiatives could serve as catalysts.

Finally, in consumer and health care, next week will reveal whether the divergence observed this week continues. The strength in UnitedHealth and other managed care names, alongside the weakness in Abbott, McCormick, and PVH, reflects a nuanced investor view of defensive and cyclical exposures. Should macro data surprise to the downside, demand for defensives could rise, but within that cohort, investors will likely remain selective, favoring those with pricing power, balance sheet strength, and clear growth drivers. For digital commerce names like Shopify and Wix, next week’s trading will show whether the market is willing to differentiate further based on execution and monetization, or whether the group trades more as a macro proxy.

## Conclusion

This week’s watchlist performance paints the picture of a market in the midst of a complex and dynamic transition. Rather than a single dominant narrative, multiple forces are at work: the continued build-out of AI infrastructure, the normalization of consumer and enterprise spending after several unusual years, the push and pull between inflation and growth in setting the macro path, and the evolving regulatory and policy environment in financials, health care, and technology. The result is high dispersion across sectors and within them, with strong double-digit moves in both directions among key names.

For portfolio managers, the implications are clear. First, broad sector or factor exposures are insufficient in such an environment; stock selection and thesis clarity are paramount. Second, risk management must recognize that many of the most attractive secular themes, such as AI and cybersecurity, are also the most volatile and sensitive to changes in rate expectations and investor sentiment. Third, diversification across complementary themes—AI infrastructure, software platforms, materials and commodities, health care services, and select industrials—can help balance portfolios against a range of macro outcomes.

The coming weeks, with a relatively light earnings calendar but a heavy backdrop of macro and policy developments, will provide an important test of the durability of the current rotations. Investors should be prepared for continued volatility and remain focused on companies with clear competitive advantages, strong balance sheets, and management teams capable of navigating a complex macro landscape. Within the watchlist, the names discussed—AMD, Micron, POET, SNDK, Western Digital, Datadog, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Arista, Shopify, Wix, Coinbase, Mosaic, Newmont, Agnico Eagle, Generac, Fortinet, UnitedHealth, Abbott, Capital One, and others—offer a rich opportunity set for expressing nuanced views on the evolving economic and market regime. The challenge and opportunity lie in calibrating exposure to each, in line with both top-down views and bottom-up conviction.

US equities saw another dispersion-heavy week, with semis, select software, and materials leading while fintech, some megacap hardware, and consumer names lagged. Within our watchlist, high-beta chip names like AMD and MU ripped higher alongside gold and fertilizer plays such as NEM, AEM, MOS and CF, even as broader financials and e‑commerce stocks came under pressure.
Macro remains in the driver’s seat, with traders toggling between soft‑landing and re‑acceleration narratives while watching real yields and dollar swings. Positioning continues to favor AI, data infrastructure, and quality healthcare, but rotations into cyclicals and commodities are becoming more pronounced. Looking ahead, the next slate of inflation prints, Fed communication, and any signs of labor cooling will shape whether this factor regime broadens beyond narrow AI leadership.
